claims.text: The baseline is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a conventional metal substrate with no preformed oxide layer and minimal native oxidation.
The controlled intervention is post-deposition annealing at approximately 300°C.
Annealing near 300°C will preferentially encourage oxidation of Cu in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The annealing treatment will produce a continuous, Cu-rich surface oxide film, potentially CuO.
A continuous Cu-rich oxide film will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
The oxide film will shift wear from severe adhesive and plastic damage toward a milder abrasive or oxidative regime.
The Cu-rich oxide film will buffer and redistribute tribological stresses.
Stress buffering by the oxide film will mitigate severe microscopic plastic deformation.
Stress buffering by the oxide film will mitigate intergranular fracture.
At the same high-temperature sliding conditions, the annealed coating will have a lower wear rate than the as-deposited coating.
At the same high-temperature sliding conditions, the annealed coating will have a lower coefficient of friction than the as-deposited coating.
The annealed coating will show milder, oxide-mediated microscopic deformation rather than pronounced plastic deformation or intergranular fracture.
Wear-resistance and friction benefits should occur in a sufficiently high-temperature sliding regime, specified as around 300°C and above.
At lower temperatures, inadequate oxide formation will prevent the predicted wear-resistance improvement.
Interactions or segregation involving Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co may alter the protective efficacy of the Cu-rich oxide film.
The hypothesis is to be tested by comparing annealed and as-deposited coatings under identical high-temperature loads and sliding speeds.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear-rate reduction and altered deformation behavior associated with a continuous Cu-rich oxide film would falsify the hypothesis.
A nonuniform oxide film or rapid oxide-film degradation during sliding would falsify the proposed continuous protective-film mechanism.
